query_text: If "Thou shalt not kill" is one of the ten commandments, why do people still kill others in the name of religion?

messages.content: If "Thou shalt not kill" is one of the ten commandments, why do people still kill others in the name of religion?

message.content:
The short answer is that the commandment is usually understood to forbid **murder**—the unjustified taking of human life—not every form of killing, and many people who kill in religion’s name are acting from **interpretation, fanaticism, power, or identity politics**, not from the core ethic of the faith itself.[2][3][5]

A few key points help explain the contradiction:

- **Religious texts are interpreted differently.** Some traditions and translators render the commandment as “You shall not murder,” emphasizing unlawful killing rather than all killing.[3]
- **People can use religion to justify preexisting motives.** Research and commentary note that some individuals use religion for status, superiority, or group dominance, and that can increase support for violence against outsiders.[1][5]
- **Many religious traditions also contain internal tensions.** Alongside anti-killing commandments, scriptures may include accounts of war, punishment, or “holy war,” which believers have sometimes used to justify violence.[2][5]
- **Religion is not the only cause.** Violence in religion’s name often overlaps with politics, ethnic conflict, revenge, or social control; religion becomes the language or banner under which those conflicts are fought.[2][5]

So the contradiction is less “religion says kill” and more “people selectively invoke religious language to legitimize violence they already want to commit.”[1][2][5]

If you want, I can also explain how Judaism, Christianity, and Islam each reconcile “do not kill” with warfare, self-defense, and capital punishment.
